title: He must increase (John 3:22–36)
hook: the Baptist, happy to fade: he must increase, I must decrease

segments.voice: Yesterday, for God so loved, read inside its night conversation. Your line was not to condemn but to save. When did you choose to help instead of judge? Day six hundred one.

Picture the founder of something. A band, a small business, a church plant. For years it was theirs, and the crowds came to them. Then someone new shows up, and the crowds start drifting over. That's where John the Baptist is now. He's still baptizing, at a place called Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there. And Jesus, not far away, is baptizing too. Well, his disciples are; John's Gospel adds a little later that Jesus himself didn't baptize. John's followers come to him worried, almost hurt: Rabbi, the one you pointed to across the Jordan, he's baptizing, and everyone is going to him.

John's answer starts with a sentence that would settle a lot of jealousy, in the King James words: "A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven." Whatever you have, you were given. Then he reminds them: I told you, I'm not the Christ, I was sent ahead of him. And then a picture from a wedding. The groom is the one with the bride. The best man, the friend of the bridegroom, isn't jealous. He stands there listening for the groom's voice, and when he hears it, he's overjoyed. "This my joy therefore is fulfilled." Then the line that gives today its name: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Must. Not a sad must, the way you'd talk about getting older. A glad one, the way you'd talk about a child growing taller than you. His whole work was pointing, and now people are going where he pointed. That's what success looks like for a pointer. Christians noticed something lovely about this line long ago. Many churches keep John the Baptist's birthday on June twenty-fourth, near the summer solstice, after which the days start getting shorter. And Christmas falls near the winter solstice, after which the days start getting longer. He must increase; I must decrease, written into the calendar and the sunlight. Augustine, in the fourth and fifth century, preached on just this. The chapter closes with words, whether John the Baptist's or the Gospel writer's, about the one who comes from above: the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.
screen: `A GLAD MUST, NOT A SAD ONE.`
then, large: `HE MUST INCREASE, BUT I MUST DECREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone else shine. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose star is rising near you. A younger colleague. A sibling. A friend whose project is taking off. Someone who might, honestly, make you a little jealous. Picture them succeeding. Notice whatever you feel: pride, envy, both. Don't scold yourself. Then try the best man's posture: standing beside them, listening, glad. Think of one thing you could do this week to help their light grow. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
He must increase. John the Baptist's answer when the crowds left him for Jesus: joy, not rivalry, like a best man hearing the groom's voice.
Your line: he must increase. Today, step back and let someone else take the credit, the spotlight or the last word, and be glad about it. Day six hundred one.

howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the birth of John the Baptist on June 24, near midsummer, and Christians often quote 'he must increase, but I must decrease' as a motto for humble service.

original.note: Greek: he must increase, grow. 'dei', must, is the word John uses for what God's plan requires.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble and step aside.
what it means: the Baptist is glad, like a best man, to fade as the one he pointed to grows, because everything is a gift from heaven.
what a scholar hears: Augustine linked 3:30 to the feasts of John (June 24) and Jesus (December 25) at the solstices; and the speaker of 3:31–36 may be the Baptist or the Gospel writer.

notes: Augustine's solstice reading of John 3:30 (e.g. Sermon 287 or 380 on the birth of John the Baptist). Confirm the sermon numbers before citing more precisely; the source entry is general.
Feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist, June 24 (Western and Eastern calendars). Confirm.
John 4:2 says Jesus himself did not baptize; mentioned to explain 3:22. Confirm.
Speaker of 3:31–36 uncertain (Baptist or evangelist); stated plainly.
Original phrase ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν (John 3:30). Confirm.

Review edit: 'The Church keeps' softened to 'many churches keep', and 'it keeps Jesus's birthday' to 'Christmas falls near the winter solstice': churches on the Julian calendar keep these feasts on other civil dates, and the solstice image is a northern-hemisphere one.
